Fifteen infantry soldiers stationed at Old Faithful started explaining the geysers to visitors. Park historians say those talks were the beginning of what rangers still do today.

August 24, 1908. A single masked man stopped stagecoach after stagecoach near Kepler Cascades. By the most-cited count he robbed seventeen of them and was never caught.

In 1903 Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone of the arch at the north entrance. In 1916 Congress created the National Park Service, and some soldiers took off their uniforms and stayed on as the first rangers.

Superintendent Norris claimed Native people were afraid of the geysers. The Park Service says the evidence shows the opposite: tribes had known this land for thousands of years.

May 7, 1894. A new law banned hunting in Yellowstone. It came too late to punish Howell, but it was written because of him. By 1902 only 23 wild bison were left.

August 24, 1877. Tourists camped near Fountain Geyser see riders appear out of the steam. Behind them, as many as 800 Nez Perce men, women and children cross the park, running from the U.S. Army.

In 1863 the United States cut the Nez Perce reservation by about ninety percent. Many never agreed to the treaty. They still call it the Thief Treaty.

About August 23, 1877, the Nez Perce entered Yellowstone near today's West Entrance, guided by Poker Joe, also called Lean Elk. Leadership was shared among several chiefs.

A party of nine tourists, most from Radersburg, Montana, came to see the geysers. The warriors took their horses and supplies and forced them to come along.

George Cowan was shot through the thigh, then in the head, and left for dead. He wasn't dead. He dragged himself about twelve miles through the forest until scouts found him on August 29.

The whole Nez Perce caravan crossed the Yellowstone River near Mud Volcano, hundreds of people and nearly two thousand horses. Today the place is called Nez Perce Ford.

General Howard followed with about 600 men and never caught up. The Nez Perce drew Sturgis away with a feint, then slipped out through a narrow gorge to the Clarks Fork River. They had spent thirteen days in Yellowstone.

In the Bears Paw Mountains, about forty miles from Canada, Army forces under Colonel Nelson Miles attacked. The siege lasted five days in freezing cold, and on October 5, 1877, Joseph handed over his rifle.

"From where the sun now stands, I will fight no more forever." The words were written down and rewritten by an Army officer. One historian counted nineteen published versions.

The survivors were not allowed to go home. They were sent to Kansas, then Oklahoma, and Joseph was never allowed to live in his Wallowa Valley again. He died in 1904.
